overview: This card’s extra-long label is a warning. From 1500 BCE, the atlas stretches four disconnected polygons from southeast Alaska and British Columbia through Washington, Oregon and much of California. It calls everyone inside “North American Pacific foraging, hunting and fishing peoples.” Real communities shared oceans, rivers, forests, trade routes and food technologies, but they were never one people, language, government or identical culture. A Tlingit camp, a Coast Salish village, a Makah community, a Nuxalk family, a Yurok river settlement and a Chumash island voyage need their own names and evidence. The map accidentally agrees: it shrinks southward in 800 CE, explodes into many named layers in 1492, returns as a smaller northern umbrella in 1500 and disappears in 1530. Those are editing seams, not mass migrations or extinction. Archaeology stays local: ancient DNA identifies salmon choices in Burrard Inlet, wet sites preserve fibre and wood, and stone-walled clam gardens reveal active sea farming. Families built homes, stored food, traveled by canoe, traded, taught children and held ceremonies. No shared pre-1530 script is securely attributable to this umbrella. Living Indigenous Nations continue; the atlas label does not.

periods.title: 1500 to 1000 BCE: four polygons replace an older umbrella
periods.summary: At 2000 BCE a broad “archaic” layer owns many tested Pacific places. In 1500 BCE this exact id appears as four disconnected components with 268 positions, stretching from southeast Alaska to California. The switch is atlas taxonomy, not the birth of coastal peoples.

periods.title: 1000 to 500 BCE: a reused shape hides many histories
periods.summary: The 1000, 700 and 500 BCE snapshots reuse the same four-part coordinate hash. Across five centuries, particular settlements, fisheries, gardens and relationships changed. A static basemap cannot turn that variation into one coast-wide culture or political border.

periods.title: 500 to 1 BCE: six files keep the same component
periods.summary: Snapshots at 500, 400, 323, 300, 200 and 100 BCE repeat the same 268-position geometry. The card therefore follows dated site evidence rather than inventing events from an unmoving outline. Local histories continued even when the editor did not redraw.

periods.title: 1 BCE to 500 CE: one tiny hash edit, no cultural reset
periods.summary: The 1 BCE file has a distinct hash although its topology, position count and bounds match the familiar shape; 100 through 500 CE return to the common hash. This decimal-level change is dataset evidence, not proof of migration, conquest or a new society.

periods.title: 500 to 800 CE: the broad southern reach continues
periods.summary: The same four-part component persists at 500, 600 and 700 CE. In 800 the feature still has four parts but loses seventy-five positions and its southern edge jumps from about 34.5 to 38.9 degrees north. That is a major editorial contraction.

periods.title: 800 to 1000 CE: southern California is reassigned
periods.summary: The 800 and 900 files share the contracted 193-position geometry. Tested Sacramento, Monterey and Morro Bay points move to an implausibly placed “anasazi” layer, while northern California remains inside this umbrella. The error warns against treating point ownership as cultural truth.

periods.title: 1000 to 1200 CE: minute edits cross three generations
periods.summary: The 1000 hash changes slightly, while 1100 and 1200 return to the earlier contracted component. All remain four-part, 193-position MultiPolygons. Archaeological dates and community histories, not tiny coordinate shifts, guide discussion of fishing, homes and exchange.

periods.title: 1200 to 1400 CE: precision wiggles, societies continue
periods.summary: The 1200 file shifts by microscopic decimals at 1279 and 1300, then changes again in 1400 without altering four-part topology or 193 positions. These hashes measure serialization differences. They do not synchronize social change across thousands of coastal kilometres.

periods.title: 1400 to 1500 CE: one umbrella becomes a named mosaic
periods.summary: The target runs from 1400 to 1492, then disappears for eight years. At 1492, many named layers own tested places, including Tlingit, Haisla, Nuxalk, Kwakwaka’wakw, Nuu-chah-nulth, Coast Salish, Makah, Chinookan, Yurok, Pomo and Chumash labels. The mosaic is also approximate.

periods.title: 1500 to 1530 CE: a smaller northern umbrella briefly returns
periods.summary: In 1500 the exact id returns with only three parts and 121 positions, ending near the central Oregon coast. A broad “coqs” label and Pomo layer own many southern points. In 1530 the umbrella vanishes into other coarse labels without a historical fall.

sections.title: Read the giant umbrella label carefully

items.text: The exact record is a circa culture entry from 1500 BCE to 1530 CE with 26 observed intervals and no existing card or summary. Its phrase describes three activities, not an Indigenous nation. Fishing, hunting and gathering were practiced by many politically and linguistically distinct peoples.

The opening geometry is one MultiPolygon with four disconnected parts and 268 positions. One part covers Prince of Wales Island, another Haida Gwaii, another Vancouver Island, and a huge mainland strip reaches California. Water between shapes did not create one government, and the outlines are not treaty boundaries.

The atlas leaves tested Prince Rupert, Victoria, the Columbia mouth, Point Reyes, San Francisco and Santa Barbara outside even when nearby places are inside. It also assigns some California points to “anasazi” in 800. These mismatches expose a rough imported basemap, not missing Indigenous history.

At 1492 the umbrella yields to dozens of names. Even “Coast Salish” means more than forty independent Nations and over twenty related but distinct languages and dialects. The dense atlas mosaic is more specific than the umbrella, yet its overlaps and modern-looking borders still require caution.

British Columbia alone contains extraordinary Indigenous language diversity, and a language-family map is an evolving community-informed depiction rather than an ancient border chart. The full Pacific footprint also includes unrelated language families farther south and north. One economy label cannot supply everybody with one vocabulary or identity.

sections.title: Discover local histories with several kinds of evidence

items.text: Olympic Peninsula sequences show changing local emphases through time: marine foods and flaked stone in some layers, then larger cedar-plank villages and differing reliance on salmon, flatfish or sea mammals. Archaeologists compare dated layers; they do not use one “Northwest Coast package” as a timeless checklist.

Kiix̣in preserves nearly three thousand years of Huu-ay-aht occupation in middens and house remains. Its standing village and fortress architecture is nineteenth-century, however. The site brilliantly joins oral history, archaeology and archives, while its different dates prevent a later defensive structure from being mislabeled 1000 BCE.

At Ozette, a mudslide sealed part of a Makah village and preserved wood, fibre, fishing gear and household objects that usually rot. The Makah Cultural and Research Center cares for and interprets the collection. Exceptional preservation reveals ordinary work without turning one village into a coast-wide template.

Ancient DNA from salmon bones at four ancestral Tsleil-Waututh settlements, dated about 400 BCE to 1200 CE, identified species and sex. Two sites favored male chum. That is strong local evidence for selective harvesting; the study’s laboratory methods do not authorize claiming every river used the same rule.

Clam-garden walls are difficult to date because beaches move sediment and old shell can be redeposited. Researchers combine radiocarbon samples, barnacle scars, shells, sea-level history and sediment evidence. On northern Quadra Island, results support about 3,500 years of use, squarely overlapping this atlas interval.

sections.title: Work with ocean, river, forest, oakland and fire

items.text: This footprint crosses stormy island coasts, fjords, salmon rivers, rain forest, estuaries, redwood country, oak woodland and drier California interiors. A Makah whaling ground, lower Columbia root place and Pomo seasonal camp demanded different calendars and skills. “Pacific” never meant one environment or identical menu.

Northern Quadra Island sea gardens used rock walls low in the intertidal zone to trap sediment, flatten beach terraces and expand clam habitat. They were engineered food landscapes, not untouched “wild” shore. Dating remains local, so the card never paints a clam wall onto every Pacific bay.

A coast-wide radiocarbon study compiled 511 dates from more than 200 wooden fish traps. Building and maintaining large traps demanded cooperation and long investment, and patterns changed with settlement and climate. The compilation reveals varied histories; it does not prove one central authority directed every fishery.

California peoples tended plants for food, medicine, shelter, clothing, tools and baskets. Acorns needed collecting, drying, pounding and repeated freshwater leaching, which is skilled processing rather than passive “foraging.” Historical syntheses help identify tasks, but individual plant use must be localized instead of projected northward.

Lower Columbia communities linked river villages, prairies, wetlands and travel corridors. Plants supported foods, medicines and artefacts, while trade moved east and west. Families followed seasonal opportunities without wandering aimlessly. Routes were social landscapes full of named places, responsibilities, partners and boundaries that this polygon cannot show.

sections.title: Catch, gather, preserve, cook and share food

items.text: Salmon mattered enormously in many northern and river communities, but species, runs, gear and rules differed by watershed. Around Sitka, archaeological and oral histories describe weirs, summer fishing camps and storage. Calling the entire coastline “salmon people” would erase whale, shellfish, acorn, seed, deer and other food systems.

Makah evidence from Ozette includes whale bones and harpoon barbs dating back about two thousand years. Specialized shafts, toggling heads, floats, ropes, paddlers, towing and butchering made whaling coordinated expertise. This is securely Makah evidence, not permission to award every coastal household a whaling canoe.

For local Miwok communities, acorns could be dried in tall granaries, pounded in mortars, leached until bitterness washed away, then cooked with hot stones in watertight baskets. It is a splendid reminder that “gathered food” can require storage engineering, chemistry, patience and a lot of stirring.

Chumash island middens preserve abalone, mussel, fish, bird and marine-mammal remains with tools and shell beads. Some water-poor islands supported seasonal visits rather than permanent villages. Bones and shells reveal meals and work, while the exact menu, sharing rule and recipe still require local context.

Fun fact: eulachon carry so much oil that a dried fish can burn like a candle, hence “candlefish.” Northern communities valued them more seriously as seasonal food and trade grease. The joke practically writes itself: useful fish, terrible birthday scent. Biology and later records do not prove identical ancient use everywhere.

sections.title: Shape wood, fibre, stone, shell and boats

items.text: Makah canoe makers hollowed cedar logs, added hot water and fire-heated stones, then spread the softened hull while preserving strong grain. Replaceable hardwood gunwales protected edges. Canoes ranged from small practice craft to ocean whalers, and navigation joined weather, stars, swells, sounds and landmarks.

Chumash tomols used carefully fitted planks, plant-fibre cord and asphaltum-based sealant rather than one hollowed log. They supported island-mainland travel and exchange, including shell beads drilled with Santa Cruz Island chert. Two excellent boat traditions demonstrate why a coast-wide “canoe type” would be false.

Coast Salish weavers later documented coiling, twining and plaiting cedar root, cedar bark, cattail, grasses and other fibres into containers, mats and garments. Some baskets held water or cooked food with heated stones. These named regional techniques are comparison, not a universal ancient craft manual.

Haida community history describes cedar canoes moving between villages, relatives, trading partners and sometimes enemies. Archaeological features include house depressions, shell middens, bark-stripped trees and lithics. Canoe travel connected sea and land, but exchange routes did not dissolve the distinct laws and identities of participating Nations.

Ozette’s wet preservation reminds us how biased survival can be. Stone and shell often last; baskets, cord, handles, wooden boxes and clothing usually disappear. When waterlogged objects survive, the “stone age” picture suddenly fills with carpentry and fibre skill. Missing wood is often rotten evidence, not missing technology.

sections.title: Build homes, store supplies and organize work

items.text: At Kiix̣in, house outlines and middens document long occupation, while surviving big-house frames belong to much later centuries. Substantial timber architecture required tree selection, carpentry, transport, raising beams, repairs and shared decisions. A permanent-looking house could still belong to a seasonal round linking several resource places.

Later Makah accounts describe winter villages with several cedar-plank longhouses, each sheltering extended families and multiple generations. Summer camps sat nearer fishing, whaling and gathering places. This local pattern shows mobility and rooted villages working together, rather than a choice between “nomad” and “settled.”

Chumash tribal history describes large dome-shaped homes made with willow branches and increasingly permanent villages supported by storage, boats and skilled work. This southern architecture differed from northern plank houses. Families used materials suited to place, so cedar should never become the umbrella card’s compulsory building code.

At Sitka, a rectangular hearth and structure dated about 1153 to 1228 CE may represent a summer house or smokehouse. Nearby pits invite several interpretations, including food caches. Radiocarbon, stratigraphy and consultation narrow possibilities, but a pit does not arrive with a label saying whose berries were inside.

Daily work included fetching water and fuel, checking tides, cutting fish, drying or smoking food, tending storage, repairing nets and traps, shaping wood, twisting fibre, preparing plants and maintaining homes. Particular people divided work differently. Archaeology preserves results more often than jokes, arguments, rest or the planning that made work possible.

sections.title: Live with family, women, children and teachers

items.text: Makah tribal history places several generations of extended family within local longhouses. Other Nations organized houses, clans, lineages, villages and leadership differently. Kin could structure access to places, names, songs or work, but this umbrella has no single marriage rule, inheritance system, chief or coast-wide family tree.

Nuxalk community maps connect families with villages of descent, crests, songs, dances and Smayustas, their histories. That evidence belongs to Nuxalk people and Country. It demonstrates why family knowledge matters, while refusing to lend Nuxalk ancestry or governance to unrelated neighbours inside the atlas polygon.

Women’s work and authority varied. Pomo women became celebrated basket makers; Chumash tribal history records women as chiefs and ceremonial specialists; fisheries and food work could involve many ages and genders. Late descriptions illuminate possibilities but cannot assign one gender chart to three millennia and thousands of kilometres.

Children learned language, places, safety, materials and relationships by listening, watching, helping and practicing with relatives. Modern Nuxalk camps and schools are explicitly present-day evidence of cultural renewal after colonial schooling disrupted family teaching. They show living pedagogy, not a reconstructed timetable for every ancient child.

Makah canoe makers produced small practice canoes for children as well as ocean craft. That gives play and learning a wonderfully concrete object: a learner could paddle, imitate and experiment at safer scale. The evidence is locally documented and later recorded, so no imaginary coast-wide “canoe class” appears here.

sections.title: Care for health, water, waste and bathroom needs

items.text: Smoke, sharp tools, cold water, storms, falls, burns, injury, infection and food shortages were possible risks, but health varied by place and century. At later Tlingit sites, spruce pitch is documented for fire starting, boat repair and medicine. That useful local comparison is not a coast-wide pharmacy.

California plant knowledge included medicines as well as food and fibre, yet broad plant lists can flatten careful expertise. A remedy depends on species, preparation, dose, season and the people authorized to use it. This card does not invent one healer title, surgery or prescription shared from Alaska to California.

Fresh water came from springs, streams, rivers, lakes, rain and carried supplies. Anacapa’s lack of dependable fresh water helps archaeologists interpret Chumash visits as seasonal; it does not reveal the exact container or ration. Water access shaped camps and voyages, but no single purification routine is securely documented here.

Middens can hold shell, bone, charcoal, broken tools and food-processing remains, sometimes building into house terraces. Archaeologists study layers, seasonality and species rather than calling every deposit a careless trash heap. Waste placement was patterned, but one midden cannot provide a universal hygiene code or daily sweeping schedule.

No built toilet, latrine, sewer or umbrella-wide bodily-waste practice is securely attributable across this exact record. People handled bathroom needs somehow, yet those traces rarely preserve or have not been identified consistently. The honest toilet report is simple: detailed fishing gear survives; a shared plumbing plan does not.

sections.title: Respect ceremony, images, language, conflict and coercion

items.text: Haida community accounts join ancestors, living beings, land, sea, villages and stewardship. Other Nations hold their own teachings, restricted knowledge and ceremonial responsibilities. The card can acknowledge spiritual relationships without translating every carving, burial or landscape feature into one generic “nature religion” invented for the umbrella.

Coast Salish carvings and basketry have archaeological depth, including Hoko River basketry about 2,500 years old. Some objects are understood as ancestors rather than Western-style “art.” Material skill, story and ceremony can meet in one object, while meaning remains with its community and context.

Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely attributable to this exact umbrella and interval. Rock markings can carry messages, memory or sacred meaning, but they are not automatically phonetic script. Borrowing a modern Haida, Nuxalk, Lushootseed, Yurok or Samala spelling would falsely make one Nation speak for all.

Conflict was real but not constant or uniform. Kiix̣in includes a nineteenth-century fortress above a site occupied since about 1000 BCE; its late date prevents backdating that structure. Defended places, weapons and trauma require local study, while trade, marriage and diplomacy also connected communities.

Later lower Columbia records document raiding, captivity and hereditary slavery, a serious form of coercion. Practices and status differed across communities, and written evidence largely postdates this card. Naming the harm matters; projecting that later system unchanged across the entire coast and all 3,000 years would also be wrong.

sections.title: Celebrate achievements, expose seams and follow continuity

items.text: Achievements were plural: selective fisheries, fish traps, clam gardens, food storage, ocean navigation, plank and dugout boats, fibre work, shell exchange, architecture, art and intergenerational law. They arose through particular communities rather than an umbrella government. Skilled abundance was produced and maintained, not simply collected from an effortless coast.

In 1492 the atlas suddenly replaces the target with a crowded mosaic of named layers. That view usefully signals diversity but mixes Nations, communities and overlapping modern-style categories. No eight-year cultural explosion occurred. The underlying peoples did not wait for a map editor to receive names, languages, laws or homelands.

In 1500 the umbrella returns as three northern components with 121 positions. Many Oregon and northern California points move beneath a broad “coqs” polygon, while Pomo owns farther-south points. The contraction is database reclassification, not a northward retreat, conquest or disappearance of coastal communities.

At 1530 the exact id vanishes. Kwakwaka’wakw, Eyak, Athabaskan, Kijkitat, Pomo, Patwin, Miwok, Costanoan and Chumash labels own some tested places, while others are blank. No synchronized fall occurred. Later epidemics, missions, land seizure and forced schooling caused real devastation, but on later local timelines.

Living Nations continue. Nuxalk families teach language on their own terms; Chumash children learn Samala and basketry; Chinook families sustain canoe and salmon traditions despite a recognition struggle. Continuity includes recovery, innovation and political work. The atlas id ends, while Indigenous peoples emphatically do not.

ending.text: The exact umbrella id disappears in 1530 as the atlas redistributes parts of the Pacific coast among named and sometimes badly overbroad labels. That file seam is not a fall, migration wave or extinction. Later colonial epidemics, missions, violence, land seizure, forced schooling and resource restrictions devastated particular Nations on different timelines. Their descendants and governments remain: they protect Country, renew languages, fish, carve, weave, paddle, teach children and correct museum and map stories today.
